description:
We are INFINITY, a team of passionate innovators, programmers, and creative thinkers united by one mission: turning bold ideas into solutions that matter.

Inspired by the endless possibilities of space and technology, we combine creativity, science, and teamwork to tackle real-world challenges using NASA's open data.

We believe that innovation has no boundaries, curiosity has no limits, and even the smallest idea can make a universe of difference.

Our mission is simple: Think beyond. Create without limits. Reach for infinity. ♾️
summary: Far from Earth is an open, browser-based toolkit for exploring the Moon and Mars, and its Earth-analog finder answers the challenge directly. We scored 104,296 land windows of 48 km covering all of Earth (80°N to 80°S) against 23 candidate Moon-base and Mars sites, among them Shackleton, de Gerlache and Faustini craters on the Moon and Jezero, Gale and Protonilus Mensae on Mars. "Analogous" is split into three scores the user can weight: terrain (slope, relief and roughness at one common 480 m scale, from NASA LOLA, MOLA and SRTM-based elevation), environment (NASA POWER temperature, precipitation, wind, UV and pressure) and ice, wind and volcanism. A 2D map and a 3D globe show a similarity heat map. Every result has a side-by-side comparison and an explicit list of what matches and where the analogy breaks down (gravity, atmosphere, radiation). A switch hides places near well-known analog sites to surface less-studied leads, such as the Kunlun plateau of north-western Tibet and the Antarctic plateau. The same site also holds a Moon and Mars route planner and a physics-based driving simulator, linked by buttons. Results are screening leads, not proof.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Far from Earth helps answer a simple question: where on Earth can we rehearse the Moon and Mars? The user picks one of 23 Moon or Mars sites. The tool scores every land window on Earth against it with three scores from 0 to 1 and combines them with weights the user sets. Terrain: median and 90th-percentile slope, relief, roughness and the whole slope distribution. Environment: mean temperature, annual temperature range, precipitation, air pressure, wind and UV index. Ice, wind and volcanism: ground-ice potential, windy-and-dry surface processes and basaltic volcanic or lava-tube setting. Results appear on a global similarity map (2D or 3D globe) and as a ranked list of distinct places at least 100 km apart. For each place the tool shows hillshades of the Moon or Mars site and of the Earth window at identical scale, the slope distributions, and a table that marks every property as a match, a partial match or a difference, with a sentence on how the place could help exploration (rover mobility, drilling in cold ground, lava-tube robots, dust studies, low-Sun navigation). Places inside the area of about 45 well-known analog sites are labelled; the rest are flagged "less-studied" and can be shown alone. The map and the selection are remembered in the page address, so a view can be shared as a link. Results download as CSV.

HOW IT WORKS

All windows (Moon, Mars, Earth) are 48 km squares resampled to 100 x 100 cells of 480 m, so slope, relief and roughness describe the same spatial scale on all three bodies. Moon and Mars windows come from the LRO LOLA 118 m and MGS MOLA 463 m elevation models around IAU feature centres. Earth windows come from open elevation tiles built from NASA SRTM and other sources, 36 km apart, giving 104,296 land windows between 80°N and 80°S. Climate comes from NASA POWER (MERRA-2) annual climatology and volcanic setting from the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program. Moon and Mars climate values are rounded literature ranges clipped to what exists on Earth, so the environment score ranks how Moon- or Mars-like a climate tendency is and never claims an exact match. Scoring runs in the browser; a Python twin builds the dataset, and an automated test confirms both give the same numbers (difference about 1e-7). A sanity check shows that well-known analog sites score high for the targets they are used for (the best score near a known site is in the top 0.3% of all windows).

WHAT WE FOUND

For ice-rich Martian mesas such as Protonilus Mensae and Deuteronilus Mensae, and for many polar lunar craters, the best less-studied matches are on the high, cold, dry, windy plateau of Kunlun in north-western Tibet. For the smooth ice-rich plains of Arcadia and Utopia the interior Antarctic plateau scores best, and for Gale crater the Puna and Altiplano of the Andes. These are leads for field study, not proof.

HONEST LIMITS

Earth cannot reproduce reduced gravity, vacuum or the thin Martian atmosphere, or the radiation environment; these are always marked as differences. The global score does not include geology, mineralogy, biology or caves. Moon and Mars environment values and the ice, aeolian and volcanic tags are hand-entered, literature-based classes that need expert review. NASA POWER is a 0.5 degree reanalysis and elevation tiles are coarser at high latitudes. The list of well-known analog sites is ours and approximate.

COMPANION TOOLS IN THE SAME PROJECT

The project also contains a layered Moon and Mars map with route planning for an astronaut on foot, a crewed rover, a robotic rover and a drone, a physics-based driving and walking simulator on the same NASA terrain, a drone, a shared multiplayer world and live NASA/JPL rover positions. The map and the Earth-analog tool are linked by buttons. These need a Python server and about 10 GB of NASA elevation data, so the repository includes screenshots and run instructions (see /routes/ on the project site).

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, Pillow), JavaScript, Leaflet, CesiumJS, three.js, FastAPI, NASA GIBS imagery, headless Chrome for screenshots, and an AI coding assistant (Claude Code).

VIDEO WALKTHROUGH
